opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to a few things that are hard for a startup to replicate, at least right now.

The first is data. Embodied intelligence doesn't have an internet's worth of free data lying around the way language models did. You have to generate it: teleoperation, real robots running in real environments, simulation at scale. That is extremely capital-intensive and operationally heavy. A large company can deploy hundreds or thousands of robots, run data collection around the clock, and absorb the cost of failure. A startup with a few dozen machines is fighting with one hand tied behind its back.

The second is compute. A foundation model means you're betting that scaling works: bigger models, more diverse data, longer training. Even if robotics models are still smaller than frontier LLMs, the iteration loop is expensive. Large companies already have the clusters, the infrastructure teams, and the experience training big models, so a lot of the engineering know-how transfers directly.

Third, and people underestimate this, is scenarios. Big companies often already own the deployment environments: warehouses, factories, logistics networks, retail, sometimes consumer hardware ecosystems. That gives them a closed loop. They deploy, collect real-world data, find failure cases, retrain, and deploy again. That flywheel is the moat. A model trained only in the lab tends to look great in demos and fall apart in the long tail of the real world.

Finally there's patience. A general-purpose robot foundation model is probably a five-to-ten-year journey before it produces a real commercial return. Large companies can treat it as a strategic bet and tolerate years without revenue. Startups face financing cycles every eighteen months and get pushed toward short-term demos or narrow commercialization.

That said, I don't think the game is decided. Big companies have their own problems: slow decision-making, organizational friction, and a tendency to bolt robotics onto existing priorities instead of going all in. The most important breakthroughs in this field may still come from small, focused teams with a strong technical insight, for example a better data recipe, a better architecture for action, or a smarter way to use video and simulation. So my view is that the large companies have the advantage in brute-force resources, but the field is still early enough that the right idea can matter more than the biggest budget.

r001.rationale: The response identifies data and compute as advantages for large companies and mentions experienced infrastructure teams, but it does not clearly attribute the advantage to a demand for world-class talent.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to three things, and they compound.

First is data. Embodied intelligence doesn't have an internet to scrape. Language models got lucky—humanity spent thirty years writing everything down for free. Robot data doesn't exist until someone pays to create it. You need fleets of robots, teleoperation setups, simulation infrastructure, people on the floor collecting demonstrations. That's a capital expense before you've trained anything. A startup might manage a few hundred hours of good data; a large company can decide to generate hundreds of thousands of hours and treat it as a line item.

Second is compute and the patience to use it. The foundation model recipe is pretraraining at scale, then seeing what emerges. For robotics, nobody is certain yet which architecture or which data mix is right, so you're running many expensive experiments that fail. Big companies can absorb a year of failed training runs. For a startup, two failed runs might be the whole company.

Third—and this is the one people underrate—is the hardware loop. You can't just train a model and ship it; the model has to live in a body, and that body has to be manufactured, maintained, and deployed somewhere real. Companies that already build cars, consumer electronics, or logistics systems have supply chains, factories, and deployment sites. They can iterate on hardware and software together. A pure software startup has to borrow or buy someone else's body, and every mismatch between the model and the hardware becomes a tax.

So the advantage isn't that large companies are smarter. It's that embodied AI is a bundle of capital-intensive problems, and the bundle gets cheaper per unit the bigger you are.

That said, I don't think it's decisive. The same was true of LLMs in 2019, and small teams still found their openings—through focus, through a specific vertical, through a hardware niche the big players ignored. What I'd tell a startup is: don't try to build the general-purpose foundation model head-on. Pick a domain where the data is naturally generated by the task itself, so the data moat grows with every deployment rather than every dollar spent.

r001.rationale: The response identifies large-scale data and compute as advantages, but its third factor is the hardware loop; it does not attribute the advantage to world-class talent.

astra-6.text:
I think their advantage comes from the resources needed to close the loop between models and the physical world. You need more than a strong algorithm. You need robots collecting data, teams maintaining the hardware, infrastructure for training, and real environments where you can test whether the model actually works.

Those pieces are expensive, and they have to improve together. A large company can fund that process for longer and coordinate people across hardware, models, and deployment. If it also has access to factories, warehouses, or other operating environments, it has somewhere to collect useful experience and measure progress.

But that advantage isn’t a guarantee. Physical-world data can be inconsistent, and collecting more of it doesn’t automatically make a better model. A smaller team with a good technical approach and a well-chosen application can still make significant progress. So I’d say large companies have an advantage in sustaining the whole development cycle; whether they turn that into a better foundation model depends on execution.

r001.rationale: The candidate mentions data collection, training infrastructure, and teams across hardware and models, but does not clearly communicate the combined demands for massive computing resources, vast amounts of data, and world-class talent.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the advantage comes from the resources you need to make the whole learning loop work. In embodied intelligence, you’re not just training on existing text or images. You need robots interacting with the physical world, collecting data, and testing whether what the model learned actually works.

Large companies can invest in hardware, computing, and teams that cover everything from models to control systems. They can also run more experiments in parallel. When a robot fails at a task, they have the capacity to collect more examples, retrain the model, and test it again. That cycle is expensive.

But resources don’t automatically produce a better model. The important question is whether a company can turn those resources into useful, diverse data and a fast learning cycle. A smaller team with a strong technical approach and a well-chosen application can still be very competitive.

r001.rationale: The response links large companies’ advantage to computing, data collection, and teams, but does not clearly state that the advantage depends on massive computing resources, vast amounts of data, and world-class talent together.
